page.title: Overview
page.intro:
Some AI companies write down how their models should behave, in a document we call a **constitution**. It is the nearest thing to a **rulebook** the public can see. For it to mean anything, it has to be **published** and **clear** enough for an independent organisation to test a model against it, and the company has to show that it trains its models on these rules and that they actually follow them. We think **every company** that builds these models should publish one, answer for what it says, and govern it properly. [More on why it matters](/about#why).

You can read every published constitution in full in the [doc reader](/doc-reader/), passage by passage, with the parts that bear on each behaviour marked. [What the constitutions say](/index) looks at **the document**: how clearly it settles conflicts between its own rules, and how deeply it covers the behaviours a model should show, a list that is not exhaustive and that we are still adding to. [How constitutions are governed](/index?view=governance) looks at **the company**: what it publishes about its constitution, and how far it holds its models to it.[1](#ovw-note-1) The method comes from working papers and Polaris Collective runs it.

notes.title: Our ambition
notes.text: We are working on two more views. How constitutions are regulated will follow how far laws and regulators refer to these documents and ask companies to keep them. Adherence of models to constitutions will carry the results of independent organisations testing whether a model actually behaves as its constitution says.

takeaways.title: Four of ten companies publish a constitution
takeaways.text: OpenAI, Anthropic, Alibaba and Microsoft AI publish one, Microsoft AI's as a draft open for public comment that its models are not yet trained on. Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI, Mistral AI, Moonshot AI and DeepSeek do not, so none of them publishes a document that sets out, in general, how the models it offers today should behave. Some publish fragments of one, such as the principles and prohibitions Google sets out for the Gemini app across several pages, the safety prompts xAI published for Grok models it has since retired, or the system prompts of Mistral AI's coding agent. The governance view counts such system prompts as a partial constitution, and with them xAI reaches the middle tier on what is published and on the final governance score. A fuller document may exist inside a company without being released, and Meta says it evaluates its Muse Spark model against one.

takeaways.title: Almost every company is weak on change
takeaways.text: In our reading, no company's public change log says in full what it covers and how soon a change is recorded, and even the best falls well short of it. We found no company that commits to warn the public before weakening one of the things its model must never do, and every weakening we found went out without notice. In August 2026 OpenAI changed a root-level rule so that every scope of autonomous action "must include an ending condition" where it had required "a shutdown timer", and its change log does not mention it. xAI in June 2026 and Meta in April 2026 loosened what their risk frameworks require before a model is developed or released, and in February 2026 Microsoft's framework stopped repeating its deeper capability assessments of a deployed model at least every six months, repeating them only when the model's risk profile changes materially.

takeaways.title: No company says which rules apply to governments and armed forces
takeaways.text: We found no company that publishes the rules its models follow once they are deployed for governments or defence. Anthropic writes that some models built for specialised uses do not fully fit its constitution, and a spokesperson has said its military models may not be trained on it. OpenAI's Model Spec distinguishes kinds of deployment, and OpenAI's post on its agreement with the Department of War says that deployment gets safety-trained models behind a safety stack OpenAI runs, without naming the Model Spec. xAI's risk framework says the full functionality of its models may be available only to trusted parties, partners and government agencies, and xAI agreed to the Pentagon's "all lawful use" standard for Grok, as Axios reported. Google confirmed in April 2026 an agreement letting the Pentagon use Gemini on classified networks. Neither has published the rules its models follow there. Microsoft AI's draft Code sends national security uses to a separate review without saying what rules apply there, and the model Microsoft offers in its Secret and Top Secret government clouds is OpenAI's GPT-5.2, which the Code does not cover. Meta opened its Llama models to NATO while their acceptable use policy still forbids military uses, and Mistral AI's usage policy does not apply to models run on a customer's own infrastructure.

takeaways.title: Three companies have agreed to write this document for a regulator, and not for the public
takeaways.text: For any model that carries systemic risk, Measure 7.1 of the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice asks the provider to give the EU AI Office a report setting out the principles the model is meant to follow, how it ranks principles and instructions, the topics it refuses and its system prompt. Three companies that publish no constitution have signed up to it: Google and Mistral AI the whole Code, and xAI its Safety and Security chapter, where Measure 7.1 sits. Microsoft has signed the whole Code as well, and has also published a draft constitution for its MAI models. The report itself is not public: the Code asks only for summaries to be published where needed, and sets no date. Mistral AI classifies none of its current models as carrying systemic risk, so on its own reading the Code asks it for no such report today. These asks belong in regulation as well as in voluntary commitments.

takeaways.title: OpenAI and Anthropic stand out, and still fall short on governance
takeaways.text: OpenAI and Anthropic are best in class on every figure. They lead every other company on how their constitutions are governed, yet neither reaches the minimum our proposal asks of a company. Alibaba is best in class on the three figures of what the constitutions say, second to OpenAI on the document as a whole, but its constitution names none of the models it governs and Alibaba is behind on all three governance figures. Microsoft AI is in the middle tier on every figure, third on governance on the strength of its absolute constraints and its open consultation, for a Code of Conduct that is still a draft its models are not trained on.

takeaways.title: The scores measure clarity and openness, not how good a model is
takeaways.text: They reward a document that states its rules explicitly and a company that shows its work. Anthropic's lower standing on the document as a whole reflects its choice to weigh its ranked values as a whole, and settings it has no rules for, such as images, audio and video. A clearer document is not proof of a better model. Microsoft AI's figures on what its constitution says are one model's provisional reading until the panel reads its Code. There is no agreed standard yet for a good constitution. This index is a first attempt at one, and we want to hear where it is wrong.

openai.profile: OpenAI publishes a constitution, the Model Spec, that is explicit throughout: it ranks every instruction by who gave it and says how firm most of its rules are. It is openly licensed and keeps its past versions. The rest of its governance is thinner, with a change log that explains changes only in part, and tests of its models against the document published once, in March 2026, and not updated for its newest models.
openai.constitutions: A strong document on both counts. It settles conflicts by rank, leaves no contradiction unsettled and covers the behaviours in depth, most of all helpfulness and judgement, and harm and safety. Its thinnest area is autonomy and oversight, including concentrations of power and secret loyalties.
openai.whole: Full marks on three criteria and close to them on a fourth. Conflicts are settled by rank, most rules say how firm they are, every situation checked has rules of its own and no contradiction stands. Reasons are the gap: they run through the safety and privacy rules and are missing from several root content rules, such as intellectual property, extremism, hate and fairness, and from the formatting rules.
openai.behaviours: Deep on helpfulness and judgement and on harm and safety, with rules and worked examples, and nearly as deep on honesty. Autonomy and oversight is its weakest category, with little on concentrations of power and secret loyalties.
openai.governance: A little over half marks. The constitution itself is public, openly licensed and versioned, and the company says the public text, though it leaves out some detail, is consistent with the behaviour it trains its models for. Testing is thin: it published one set of adherence tests in March 2026 and has not kept it current, none of its outside evaluators tests adherence to the Model Spec, and no threshold decides whether a model is released.
openai.published: The Model Spec is public under an open licence, at a dated address with all its past versions, and says what it covers. The change log, the guardrails and the hard constraints are documented only in part, and it names kinds of deployment without saying whether government use is among those it governs.
openai.engages: Strong on use: it says how its public text relates to the one it trains on, and models are monitored in use. Training on the document is described in detail only for an earlier generation of models. Change control is partial. Testing is thin: one set of adherence tests, published in March 2026 and not kept current, outside evaluators who test other risks, and no threshold that decides whether a model is released.

anthropic.profile: Anthropic publishes Claude's Constitution, a long document that explains its reasons and covers the behaviours in depth, while applying the order of its core values holistically rather than strictly, by design. It is openly licensed, says which models it covers, and the company says its models are trained on it. It keeps no change log for it, and little is published on testing.
anthropic.constitutions: Deep on the behaviours and less explicit as a document. It covers harm, helpfulness and oversight in depth, but it applies the order of its values holistically by design, so it rarely says in advance how a given conflict resolves.
anthropic.whole: Its strength is reasons: nearly every rule says why it exists. It is weaker on which rule wins, on how firm each rule is and on the situations it covers, partly because it is written to leave room for judgement. Images, audio and video have no rules of their own.
anthropic.behaviours: Deep on helpfulness and judgement and on harm and safety. Honesty and epistemics is its lowest category, held down by sycophancy and contested questions, and within autonomy and oversight it says least about secret loyalties.
anthropic.governance: A little over half marks. The constitution is public, openly licensed and says which models it covers, and the company says its models are trained on it and that the same text is used inside. The constitution has no change log, though its earlier version is still online and the company has committed to update the public text within 90 days of deploying a model trained on a newer one. Nothing is published on change control, and testing is thinly documented: a claim of adherence with no method, and outside evaluators who test other risks.
anthropic.published: The constitution is public under an open licence, says which models it covers and lists its hard constraints in full. Its record of changes is the weak point: the constitution has no change log and no version number, its 2023 version is still online with no link back to it, and nothing records later edits, though the company has committed to update the public text within 90 days of deploying a model trained on a newer one.
anthropic.engages: Strong on training and use: models are trained on the constitution, the same text is used inside and models are monitored in use. Nothing is published on change control, and little on testing against the document: a claim of adherence with no method, and outside evaluators who test other risks.

notes.whole: This row averages five criteria. Claude's Constitution chooses to rank its values and leave their application to the model's judgement, which lowers its figures on which rule wins and on how firm each rule is. It also has no rules for images, audio or video. We prefer clarity, because it is what lets anyone test a model against what its constitution says. That preference is ours, and it is open to challenge.

alibaba.profile: Alibaba's Model Spec is a well-built rulebook that settles conflicts explicitly. It is published by Alibaba's AI governance laboratory in the company's name, and it names no model it governs. Almost nothing is published about how it is maintained. Alibaba says it is training its models towards it, and its lab has built one research model on it and scored two Qwen models against it, neither from the current Qwen line.
alibaba.constitutions: A strong document. It is explicit about which rule wins between levels, its rules are firm and no contradiction is left unsettled, and it covers helpfulness and honesty well. Its gaps are reasons, which are brief and missing from its hard prohibitions, and autonomy and oversight, especially secret loyalties.
alibaba.whole: Clear about which rule wins between levels and how firm each rule is, with rules for nearly every situation checked and no unsettled contradiction. Reasons are its weak point: most rules give one in a single clause, and its hard prohibitions give none.
alibaba.behaviours: Deep on helpfulness and judgement, and good on honesty and on harm and safety. Autonomy and oversight is its weakest category, with very little on secret loyalties.
alibaba.governance: Low. The document is public and lists its hard constraints, though some are set by policy documents it does not publish. It names no model it covers, though it implies that it governs Alibaba's production models, has no change log, and says it is open source without naming a licence. The guardrails of its own model platform are listed by category. Its lab has published scores against it for two Qwen models that stop before the current line, and nothing is published on who approves a change.
alibaba.published: The constitution is public and lists its hard constraints, though some are set by policy documents it does not publish. It names no model it covers, though it implies that it governs Alibaba's production models, keeps no change log and says it is open source without naming a licence. The guardrails of its own model platform are listed by category, with no list for its apps.
alibaba.engages: A little on training and testing. The document says Alibaba is training its models towards it, and that its values match internal standards though the public text leaves out detail. Its lab has published scores against it for two Qwen models that stop before the current line. Nothing is published on monitoring or on who approves a change.
alibaba.caveat: It was published in Alibaba's name on the site of its AI governance laboratory (AAIG). It says Alibaba is training its models towards it and names none of them. As of September 2026, the only model we found publicly built on it is Oyster-II, a research model built on Qwen3-14B, and the same release scores Qwen3-Max and Qwen3.5-397B against it.

microsoft.profile: Microsoft AI publishes a constitution for its MAI models, the Humanist AI Code of Conduct, as a draft open for public comment that it says its models are not yet trained on. The Code puts safety and human control above its other objectives and lists ten constraints nobody can override. Around it little is published: no change log, no licence, and tests of one model against the company's own safety policies rather than against the Code.
microsoft.constitutions: A middle figure on both counts, from a provisional reading by one model. The Code says which rules come first, safety and human control, and leaves clashes below that to judgement, three of which stand unsettled. It covers honesty in depth and gives most behaviours quotable rules with one worked case or none.
microsoft.whole: Clear on which rules come first and on the force of each part, with reasons for most sections and rules for every situation checked, images, audio and video only thinly. It loses most on contradictions: three clashes between guidelines of the same rank have nothing to say which prevails, which puts that criterion at zero.
microsoft.behaviours: Deepest on honesty, with rules and worked cases. Most other behaviours have quotable rules and one worked case or none, and preventing secret loyalties and avoiding concentrations of power are only named, in rules about other things.
microsoft.governance: Below half marks. The Code is public, lists its absolute constraints and was opened for comment with a promise to consult on new versions. It is a draft not yet in force, with no change log and no licence, and one of its models is tested against the company's own safety policies rather than against the Code.
microsoft.published: The Code is public and lists its ten absolute constraints, and its consultation is open to anyone, with a promise to consult again on new versions. It carries one date and no version number, change log or licence, its coverage counts only as implied while it is a draft, and its guardrails are listed by category for one platform only.
microsoft.engages: The Code is not yet used to train the models, and nothing is published on who may change it. The company tests one of its models against its own safety policies and gates each release on those tests, and outside testers have assessed its models for other risks.

google.profile: Google DeepMind publishes no constitution. What it says about how Gemini should behave is spread across several documents with different owners, and it describes the guardrails it offers developers in detail. It keeps little record of how these rules change, and its model cards test each current model against the safety policies they list.
google.governance: Low. There is no single constitution, a detailed account of developer guardrails and almost no record of changes to the rules. Its model cards test each current model against the safety policies they list and say each met a launch threshold for child safety, and it describes some outside testing, training and monitoring.
google.published: No single constitution: its rules for the Gemini app are spread across several documents, and its model cards tie its safety policies to named models. The guardrails it offers developers are described in detail. It refers to a set of harms that are always blocked without listing them, and keeps little record of changes.
google.engages: Its model cards publish tests of each current model against the safety policies they list, and say each met a launch threshold for child safety without publishing its level. It uses outside testers and describes some training and monitoring. Nothing is published on who approves a change to the rules.

mistral.profile: Mistral AI publishes no constitution. It publishes the system prompts of its coding agent, which rank instructions and mark a few as not overridable, with every change visible line by line, and it documents in detail the guardrails it offers developers. Nothing is published on training or testing its models against written rules.
mistral.governance: Low. Its points come from the system prompts of its coding agent, which the governance view counts as a partial constitution, with their history line by line and a short list of approvals marked as not overridable, and from the guardrails it offers developers. Nothing is published on training, testing or change control.
mistral.published: No constitution. It publishes the system prompts of its coding agent under an open licence, with every change shown line by line, and they mark a short list of approvals as not overridable. The guardrails it offers developers are well described, with some record of their changes.
mistral.engages: Nothing found on training, testing or change control.

meta.profile: Meta publishes no constitution, but has committed in writing to publish one. It says more about testing and training its models than about any written rules.
meta.governance: Low. Little is published about its rules, though it lists by kind the guardrails of its Muse agent, describes those it offers developers and announces some changes to its safeguards in its newsroom. It publishes adherence testing against an internal specification, and describes outside testers and training against internal policies.
meta.published: Little: no constitution and no list of hard constraints, a short record of versions of its framework, fragments of intended behaviour in a template prompt and rules for teenagers, and guardrails described for developers and listed by kind for its Muse agent, with some changes to them announced in its newsroom.
meta.engages: Some published adherence testing against an internal specification, outside testers, and training and monitoring against internal policies. It names who confirms changes to its risk framework and nobody for a document on how its models behave.

xai.profile: xAI publishes no constitution. The rules it has published for its models are system prompts for models it has since retired, and what it describes of its guardrails and testing is partial.
xai.governance: Low. It published safety prompts for models it has since retired, with a log that shows each change line by line, and gives partial accounts of its guardrails, announcing some changes to them on X. It acknowledges that government agencies may get fuller functionality, without saying what rules apply there. Its model cards test Grok against a refusal policy published only for those retired models, and an outside testing agreement has produced no published result.
xai.published: No constitution. A list of disallowed activities, marked as overriding every other instruction, was published for its 2025 API models, since retired, and its log of prompt changes, which shows each change line by line, stopped in November 2025. It gives a partial account of its guardrails, announces some changes to them on X, and says government agencies may get fuller functionality without saying what rules apply.
xai.engages: Its model cards test how often Grok complies with requests its refusal policy says to refuse, and it describes training and monitoring against that policy, which is published only for models since retired. It signed an outside testing agreement that has produced no published result. On change control there is only a 2025 statement that prompt changes need review, with no approver named.

moonshot.profile: Moonshot AI publishes no constitution: the nearest thing is a default system prompt in its developer guide. Little is published about its rules, how they change or how its models are held to them.
moonshot.governance: Very low. A sample system prompt, dated terms with no record of what changed, a description of the content filter on its API and in its app, and a 2025 red-team, tied to no behaviour document, of a model since withdrawn.
moonshot.published: No constitution, only a sample system prompt in its developer guide. Its terms are dated, with no record of what changed, and it describes the content filter on its API and in its app.
moonshot.engages: Almost nothing: a description of some training against internal policies. Its one published safety test, a red-team of a model since withdrawn, is tied to no behaviour document, and nothing is published on change control.

deepseek.profile: DeepSeek publishes no constitution. Beyond a disclosure page of the kind its regulator requires and its R1 paper of 2025, almost nothing is published on how its models are governed.
deepseek.governance: Very low: the disclosure its regulator requires, a contractual right to filter inputs and outputs, and a paper of 2025 that describes the safety training, the risk control system and a safety evaluation of its R1 model. Nothing of the kind has been published for later models.
deepseek.published: No constitution. Beyond the disclosure its regulator requires, there is its R1 paper of 2025, which describes its safety training and its risk control system, and the system prompts of two models, published in their 2025 model cards.
deepseek.engages: A description of training against an internal policy, and a safety evaluation of R1, a model it no longer serves, against its own standards.

context.name: For context
context.plain: Two facts about each company that no figure of the index counts: how capable its most capable model is, and how many people the company says use it. They are here to show what is at stake, and they change nothing above.
context.note: These rows show how capable each company's best model is and roughly how widely its models are used. A published, well-governed constitution matters more as both grow. They count towards no score, and each cell says where its figure comes from.

rows.name: Most capable model
rows.plain: The model the company builds itself that scores highest on the Epoch Capabilities Index, which combines more than fifty benchmarks into one scale of general capability, shown as how many months it trails the most capable model Epoch rates. Epoch finds that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year on its index since reasoning models arrived, so we read a gap in points as that much time. It measures capability, not danger, and a gap of a few months is within the index's own margin. "Open weights" under it means anyone can download that model and run it where the company cannot see how it is used.
rows.source: Epoch AI, Epoch Capabilities Index, as of 28 September 2026
rows.what: The model the company builds itself that scores highest on the Epoch Capabilities Index, which combines more than fifty benchmarks into one scale of general capability, shown as how many months it trails the most capable model Epoch rates. "Open weights" under it means anyone can download that model and run it where the company cannot see how it is used.
rows.from: Epoch AI's Epoch Capabilities Index, data of 28 September 2026, published under CC BY 4.0. The months come from Epoch's finding that, since reasoning models arrived in September 2024, the frontier has gained about 14 points a year on its index.
rows.limits: It measures capability on benchmarks. It says nothing about how a model behaves or how dangerous it is. Reading a gap in points as months is ours, and models a few months apart are within the index's own margin. Epoch rates only the models it has tested, which leaves out Microsoft AI's.

rows.name: Usage
rows.plain: A rough idea of how widely the company's models are used, from none to three squares. It is our own estimate and very subjective.
rows.what: A rough idea of how widely each company's models are used, in three squares: all three filled for hundreds of millions of people a month, two for tens of millions or a large place among developers, one for less. Three empty squares mean we have nothing to go on.
rows.from: Our own reading of scattered signals: the user counts companies state, their share of developer traffic on OpenRouter, downloads of their open models and outside estimates. Each cell lists the signals behind it.
rows.limits: It is very subjective. No source counts every company the same way, most companies publish no comparable figure, and two careful readers could place several companies a step apart. It gives an idea of scale and should be read that way.

capability.text: GPT-6 Astra, released on 3 September 2026, scores 166.6 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 163.0 to 172.0. Its weights cannot be downloaded. That puts it at the frontier: no model Epoch rates is ahead of it by more than the index's own margin.

usage.text: OpenAI said on 6 August 2026 that 1 billion people a week use ChatGPT.

capability.text: Claude Fable 5.1, released on 1 September 2026, scores 165.0 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 161.6 to 169.6. Its weights cannot be downloaded. That puts it at the frontier: no model Epoch rates is ahead of it by more than the index's own margin.

usage.text: Anthropic states no count of the people who use Claude. Its chief product officer said in March 2026 that more than a million people were signing up for Claude every day, and its models had the fourth largest share of developer traffic on OpenRouter in September 2026, 3.9%.

capability.text: Qwen 3.8 Max, released on 2 August 2026, scores 156.7 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 154.6 to 159.0. Its weights cannot be downloaded. That is about 8 months behind the most capable model Epoch rates, reading Epoch's finding that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year.

usage.text: Alibaba said in its annual report of 20 May 2026 that consumer-facing Qwen passed 295 million monthly active users in March 2026.

capability.text: Epoch rates no model Microsoft AI has built. The one Microsoft model it rates is Phi-4, a Microsoft Research model released in December 2024, at 130.4.

usage.text: Microsoft AI's own models are barely deployed yet. It states no count for them, and the Copilot assistants Microsoft counts run mostly on models it licenses rather than builds.

capability.text: Gemini 3.7 Flash, released on 13 August 2026, scores 157.7 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 155.6 to 160.6. Its weights cannot be downloaded. That is about 8 months behind the most capable model Epoch rates, reading Epoch's finding that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year.

usage.text: Google said on 11 August 2026 that the Gemini app had passed 1 billion monthly users.

capability.text: Mistral Medium 3.5, released on 28 April 2026, scores 141.4 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 138.6 to 143.5. Its weights can be downloaded, for restricted use. That is about 22 months behind the most capable model Epoch rates, reading Epoch's finding that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year.

usage.text: Mistral AI states no count of its users. Its app passed a million downloads in February 2025, and its models took 0.2% of developer traffic on OpenRouter in September 2026.

capability.text: Muse Spark 1.3, released on 2 September 2026, scores 156.9 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 154.7 to 159.4. Its weights cannot be downloaded. That is about 8 months behind the most capable model Epoch rates, reading Epoch's finding that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year.

usage.text: Meta said on 29 October 2025 that more than a billion monthly actives use Meta AI, which runs inside Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger. The figure is old, and Meta has given none since.

capability.text: Grok 4.6, released on 12 August 2026, scores 156.5 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 154.6 to 159.0. Its weights cannot be downloaded. That is about 9 months behind the most capable model Epoch rates, reading Epoch's finding that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year.

usage.text: About 117 million monthly active users used Grok's AI features on 31 March 2026, in a prospectus that counts Grok used inside X.

capability.text: Kimi K3, released on 16 July 2026, scores 157.7 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 155.1 to 160.7. Its weights can be downloaded, for non-commercial use. That is about 8 months behind the most capable model Epoch rates, reading Epoch's finding that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year.

usage.text: Moonshot AI last stated a count in 2024, 36 million monthly users of Kimi. Its models took 1.5% of developer traffic on OpenRouter in September 2026.

capability.text: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813, released on 13 August 2026, scores 155.4 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 153.7 to 157.3. Its weights can be downloaded by anyone. That is about 10 months behind the most capable model Epoch rates, reading Epoch's finding that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year.

usage.text: DeepSeek states no count of the people who use its assistant. Its models had the largest share of developer traffic on OpenRouter in September 2026, 21.4%, and its open models are among the most downloaded.
